# rayon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rayon/^1/

## Expand description

Rayon is a data-parallelism library that makes it easy to convert sequential computations into parallel.

It is lightweight and convenient for introducing parallelism into existing code. It guarantees data-race free executions and takes advantage of parallelism when sensible, based on work-load at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-rayon)How to use Rayon

There are two ways to use Rayon:

- **High-level parallel constructs**are the simplest way to use Rayon and also typically the most efficient.- [Parallel iterators](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)make it easy to convert a sequential iterator to execute in parallel.- The `ParallelIterator`
- The `IndexedParallelIterator`

- The
- The `par_sort``&mut [T]`slices (or vectors) in parallel.
- `par_extend`

- **Custom tasks**let you divide your work into parallel tasks yourself.- `join`
- `scope`
- `ThreadPoolBuilder`

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-and-the-rayon-prelude)Basic usage and the Rayon prelude

First, you will need to add `rayon` to your `Cargo.toml`.

Next, to use parallel iterators or the other high-level methods,
you need to import several traits. Those traits are bundled into
the module [ rayon::prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html). It is recommended that you import
all of these traits at once by adding

`use rayon::prelude::*` at
the top of each module that uses Rayon methods.These traits give you access to the `par_iter` method which provides
parallel implementations of many iterative functions such as [ map](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.map),

[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.for_each)

`for_each`[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.filter)

`filter`[, and](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.fold)

`fold`[more](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#provided-methods).

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-layout)Crate Layout

Rayon extends many of the types found in the standard library with
parallel iterator implementations. The modules in the `rayon`
crate mirror [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html) itself: so, e.g., the

`option` module in
Rayon contains parallel iterators for the `Option` type, which is
found in [the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/index.html). Similarly, the

`option` module of `std``collections` module in Rayon offers parallel iterator types for
[the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/index.html). You will rarely need to access these submodules unless you need to name iterator types explicitly.

`collections` from `std`[§](https://docs.rs#targets-without-threading)Targets without threading

Rayon has limited support for targets without `std` threading implementations.
See the [ rayon_core](https://docs.rs/rayon-core/1.13.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rayon_core/index.html) documentation for more information about its global fallback.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-questions)Other questions?

See [the Rayon FAQ](https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/main/FAQ.md).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [broadcast](https://docs.rs/fn.broadcast.html)
- Executes `op`within every thread in the current thread pool. If this is called from a non-Rayon thread, it will execute in the global thread pool. Any attempts to use`join`,`scope`, or parallel iterators will then operate within that thread pool. When the call has completed on each thread, returns a vector containing all of their return values.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the number of threads in the current registry. If this code is executing within a Rayon thread pool, then this will be the number of threads for the thread pool of the current thread. Otherwise, it will be the number of threads for the global thread pool.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_thread_index.html)- thread_ - index
- If called from a Rayon worker thread, returns the index of that
thread within its current pool; if not called from a Rayon thread,
returns `None`.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope.html)- place_ - scope
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope_fifo.html)- place_ - scope_ - fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [join](https://docs.rs/fn.join.html)
- Takes two closures and *potentially*runs them in parallel. It returns a pair of the results from those closures.
- [join_](https://docs.rs/fn.join_context.html)- context
- Identical to `join`, except that the closures have a parameter that provides context for the way the closure has been called, especially indicating whether they’re executing on a different thread than where`join_context`was called. This will occur if the second job is stolen by a different thread, or if`join_context`was called from outside the thread pool to begin with.
- [max_](https://docs.rs/fn.max_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the maximum number of threads that Rayon supports in a single thread pool.
- [scope](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [scope_](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)- fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [spawn](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn.html)
- Puts the task into the Rayon thread pool’s job queue in the “static”
or “global” scope. Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)to create a scope.`scope()`function
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_broadcast.html)- broadcast
- Spawns an asynchronous task on every thread in this thread pool. This task
will run in the implicit, global scope, which means that it may outlast the
current stack frame – therefore, it cannot capture any references onto the
stack (you will likely need a `move`closure).
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_fifo.html)- fifo
- Fires off a task into the Rayon thread pool in the “static” or
“global” scope.  Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)to create a scope.`scope_fifo()`function
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_local.html)- local
- Cooperatively yields execution to local Rayon work.
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_now.html)- now
- Cooperatively yields execution to Rayon.

# tar - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tar/^0.4.16/

## Expand description

A library for reading and writing TAR archives

This library provides utilities necessary to manage [TAR archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tar_%28computing%29)
abstracted over a reader or writer. Great strides are taken to ensure that
an archive is never required to be fully resident in memory, and all objects
provide largely a streaming interface to read bytes from.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

When unpacking archives ([ Archive::unpack](https://docs.rs/struct.Archive.html#method.unpack),

[), a best-effort is made to prevent writing files outside the destination directory: paths containing](https://docs.rs/struct.Entry.html#method.unpack_in)

`Entry::unpack_in``..` are rejected, and symlink targets within
the archive are validated before use.**Concurrent mutation of the destination tree is outside the threat model.**
If another process modifies the destination (for example, by atomically
swapping a symlink) while extraction is in progress, this crate may follow
a path outside the intended destination. Preventing such TOCTOU races
requires OS primitives (e.g. `openat`/`O_PATH` used throughout) that this
crate does not use. When extracting untrusted archives in an environment
where the destination may be concurrently modified, use the [ cap-std](https://docs.rs/cap-std/)
crate and/or OS-level sandboxing.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Archive](https://docs.rs/struct.Archive.html)
- A top-level representation of an archive file.
- [Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html)
- A structure for building archives
- [Entries](https://docs.rs/struct.Entries.html)
- An iterator over the entries of an archive.
- [Entry](https://docs.rs/struct.Entry.html)
- A read-only view into an entry of an archive.
- [Entry](https://docs.rs/struct.EntryWriter.html)- Writer
- A writer for a single entry in a tar archive.
- [GnuExt](https://docs.rs/struct.GnuExtSparseHeader.html)- Sparse - Header
- Representation of the entry found to represent extended GNU sparse files.
- [GnuHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.GnuHeader.html)
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive
- [GnuSparse](https://docs.rs/struct.GnuSparseHeader.html)- Header
- Description of the header of a sparse entry.
- [Header](https://docs.rs/struct.Header.html)
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive
- [OldHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.OldHeader.html)
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive
- [PaxExtension](https://docs.rs/struct.PaxExtension.html)
- A key/value pair corresponding to a pax extension.
- [PaxExtensions](https://docs.rs/struct.PaxExtensions.html)
- An iterator over the pax extensions in an archive entry.
- [Ustar](https://docs.rs/struct.UstarHeader.html)- Header
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Entry](https://docs.rs/enum.EntryType.html)- Type
- Indicate the type of content described by a header.
- [Header](https://docs.rs/enum.HeaderMode.html)- Mode
- Declares the information that should be included when filling a Header from filesystem metadata.
- [Unpacked](https://docs.rs/enum.Unpacked.html)
- When unpacking items the unpacked thing is returned to allow custom additional handling by users. Today the File is returned, in future the enum may be extended with kinds for links, directories etc.

- A deterministic, arbitrary, non-zero timestamp that use used as `mtime`of headers when`HeaderMode::Deterministic`

# walkdir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/walkdir/^2.3.2/

## Expand description

Crate `walkdir` provides an efficient and cross platform implementation
of recursive directory traversal. Several options are exposed to control
iteration, such as whether to follow symbolic links (default off), limit the
maximum number of simultaneous open file descriptors and the ability to
efficiently skip descending into directories.

To use this crate, add `walkdir` as a dependency to your project’s
`Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
walkdir = "2"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#from-the-top)From the top

The [ WalkDir](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html) type builds iterators. The

[type describes values yielded by the iterator. Finally, the](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)

`DirEntry`[type is a small wrapper around](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)

`Error`[with additional information, such as if a loop was detected while following symbolic links (not enabled by default).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/struct.Error.html)

`std::io::Error`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following code recursively iterates over the directory given and prints the path for each entry:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo") {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
Or, if you’d like to iterate over all entries and ignore any errors that
may arise, use [ filter_map](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.filter_map). (e.g., This code below will silently skip
directories that the owner of the running process does not have permission to
access.)

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter().filter_map(|e| e.ok()) {
    println!("{}", entry.path().display());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-follow-symbolic-links)Example: follow symbolic links

The same code as above, except [ follow_links](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.follow_links) is enabled:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").follow_links(true) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-skip-hidden-files-and-directories-on-unix)Example: skip hidden files and directories on unix

This uses the [ filter_entry](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html#method.filter_entry) iterator adapter to avoid yielding hidden files
and directories efficiently (i.e. without recursing into hidden directories):

```
use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
    entry.file_name()
         .to_str()
         .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
         .unwrap_or(false)
}
let walker = WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter();
for entry in walker.filter_entry(|e| !is_hidden(e)) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DirEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)
- A directory entry.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error produced by recursively walking a directory.
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterEntry.html)- Entry
- A recursive directory iterator that skips entries.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator for recursively descending into a directory.
- [WalkDir](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html)
- A builder to create an iterator for recursively walking a directory.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [DirEntry](https://docs.rs/trait.DirEntryExt.html)- Ext
- Unix-specific extension methods for `walkdir::DirEntry`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A result type for walkdir operations.

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/syn/latest/target-redirect/syn/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaNameValue.html)- Name - Value - `derive`or- `full`
- A name-value pair within an attribute, like `feature = "nightly"`.
- [Parenthesized](https://docs.rs/struct.ParenthesizedGenericArguments.html)- Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Arguments of a function path segment: the `(A, B) -> C`in`Fn(A,B) -> C`.
- [PatConst](https://docs.rs/struct.PatConst.html)- `full`
- A const block: `const { ... }`.
- [PatIdent](https://docs.rs/struct.PatIdent.html)- `full`
- A pattern that binds a new variable: `ref mut binding @ SUBPATTERN`.
- [PatLit](https://docs.rs/struct.PatLit.html)- `full`
- A literal in place of an expression: `1`,`"foo"`.
- [PatMacro](https://docs.rs/struct.PatMacro.html)- `full`
- A macro invocation expression: `format!("{}", q)`.
- [PatOr](https://docs.rs/struct.PatOr.html)- `full`
- A pattern that matches any one of a set of cases.
- [PatParen](https://docs.rs/struct.PatParen.html)- `full`
- A parenthesized pattern: `(A | B)`.
- [PatPath](https://docs.rs/struct.PatPath.html)- `full`
- A path like `core::mem::replace`possibly containing generic parameters and a qualified self-type.
- [PatRange](https://docs.rs/struct.PatRange.html)- `full`
- A range expression: `1..2`,`1..`,`..2`,`1..=2`,`..=2`.
- [PatReference](https://docs.rs/struct.PatReference.html)- `full`
- A reference pattern: `&mut var`.
- [PatRest](https://docs.rs/struct.PatRest.html)- `full`
- The dots in a tuple or slice pattern: `[0, 1, ..]`.
- [PatSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.PatSlice.html)- `full`
- A dynamically sized slice pattern: `[a, b, ref i @ .., y, z]`.
- [PatStruct](https://docs.rs/struct.PatStruct.html)- `full`
- A struct or struct variant pattern: `Variant { x, y, .. }`.
- [PatTuple](https://docs.rs/struct.PatTuple.html)- `full`
- A tuple pattern: `(a, b)`.
- [PatTuple](https://docs.rs/struct.PatTupleStruct.html)- Struct - `full`
- A tuple struct or tuple variant pattern: `Variant(x, y, .., z)`.
- [PatType](https://docs.rs/struct.PatType.html)- `full`
- A type ascription pattern: `foo: f64`.
- [PatWild](https://docs.rs/struct.PatWild.html)- `full`
- A pattern that matches any value: `_`.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.Path.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A path at which a named item is exported (e.g. `alloc::collections::HashMap`).
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.PathSegment.html)- Segment - `derive`or- `full`
- A segment of a path together with any path arguments on that segment.
- [Precise](https://docs.rs/struct.PreciseCapture.html)- Capture - `full`
- Precise capturing bound: the ‘use<…>’ in `impl Trait + use<'a, T>`.
- [Predicate](https://docs.rs/struct.PredicateLifetime.html)- Lifetime - `derive`or- `full`
- A lifetime predicate in a `where`clause:`'a: 'b + 'c`.
- [Predicate](https://docs.rs/struct.PredicateType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A type predicate in a `where`clause:`for<'c> Foo<'c>: Trait<'c>`.
- [QSelf](https://docs.rs/struct.QSelf.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The explicit Self type in a qualified path: the `T`in`<T as Display>::fmt`.
- [Receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)- `full`
- The `self`argument of an associated method.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.Signature.html)- `full`
- A function signature in a trait or implementation: `unsafe fn initialize(&self)`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/struct.StmtMacro.html)- Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation in statement position.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitBound.html)- Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemConst.html)- Item - Const - `full`
- An associated constant within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemFn.html)- Item - Fn - `full`
- An associated function within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemMacro.html)- Item - Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemType.html)- Item - Type - `full`
- An associated type within the definition of a trait.
- [Turbofish](https://docs.rs/struct.Turbofish.html)- `printing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Returned by `TypeGenerics::as_turbofish`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeArray.html)- Array - `derive`or- `full`
- A fixed size array type: `[T; n]`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeBareFn.html)- Bare - Fn - `derive`or- `full`
- A bare function type: `fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeGenerics.html)- Generics - `printing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Returned by `Generics::split_for_impl`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeGroup.html)- Group - `derive`or- `full`
- A type contained within invisible delimiters.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeImplTrait.html)- Impl - Trait - `derive`or- `full`
- An `impl Bound1 + Bound2 + Bound3`type where`Bound`is a trait or a lifetime.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeInfer.html)- Infer - `derive`or- `full`
- Indication that a type should be inferred by the compiler: `_`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeMacro.html)- Macro - `derive`or- `full`
- A macro in the type position.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeNever.html)- Never - `derive`or- `full`
- The never type: `!`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A generic type parameter: `T: Into<String>`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeParen.html)- Paren - `derive`or- `full`
- A parenthesized type equivalent to the inner type.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypePath.html)- Path - `derive`or- `full`
- A path like `core::slice::Iter`, optionally qualified with a self-type as in`<Vec<T> as SomeTrait>::Associated`.
- [TypePtr](https://docs.rs/struct.TypePtr.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A raw pointer type: `*const T`or`*mut T`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeReference.html)- Reference - `derive`or- `full`
- A reference type: `&'a T`or`&'a mut T`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeSlice.html)- Slice - `derive`or- `full`
- A dynamically sized slice type: `[T]`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeTraitObject.html)- Trait - Object - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait object type `dyn Bound1 + Bound2 + Bound3`where`Bound`is a trait or a lifetime.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeTuple.html)- Tuple - `derive`or- `full`
- A tuple type: `(A, B, C, String)`.
- [UseGlob](https://docs.rs/struct.UseGlob.html)- `full`
- A glob import in a `use`item:`*`.
- [UseGroup](https://docs.rs/struct.UseGroup.html)- `full`
- A braced group of imports in a `use`item:`{A, B, C}`.
- [UseName](https://docs.rs/struct.UseName.html)- `full`
- An identifier imported by a `use`item:`HashMap`.
- [UsePath](https://docs.rs/struct.UsePath.html)- `full`
- A path prefix of imports in a `use`item:`core::...`.
- [UseRename](https://docs.rs/struct.UseRename.html)- `full`
- An renamed identifier imported by a `use`item:`HashMap as Map`.
- [Variadic](https://docs.rs/struct.Variadic.html)- `full`
- The variadic argument of a foreign function.
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/struct.Variant.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An enum variant.
- [VisRestricted](https://docs.rs/struct.VisRestricted.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A visibility level restricted to some path: `pub(self)`or`pub(super)`or`pub(crate)`or`pub(in some::module)`.
- [Where](https://docs.rs/struct.WhereClause.html)- Clause - `derive`or- `full`
- A `where`clause in a definition:`where T: Deserialize<'de>, D: 'static`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attr](https://docs.rs/enum.AttrStyle.html)- Style - `derive`or- `full`
- Distinguishes between attributes that decorate an item and attributes that are contained within an item.
- [BinOp](https://docs.rs/enum.BinOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operator: `+`,`+=`,`&`.
- [Captured](https://docs.rs/enum.CapturedParam.html)- Param - `full`
- Single parameter in a precise capturing bound.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/enum.Data.html)- `derive`
- The storage of a struct, enum or union data structure.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A Rust expression.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/enum.FieldMutability.html)- Mutability - `derive`or- `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Fields](https://docs.rs/enum.Fields.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Data stored within an enum variant or struct.
- [FnArg](https://docs.rs/enum.FnArg.html)- `full`
- An argument in a function signature: the `n: usize`in`fn f(n: usize)`.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/enum.ForeignItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an `extern`block.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericArgument.html)- Argument - `derive`or- `full`
- An individual generic argument, like `'a`,`T`, or`Item = T`.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A generic type parameter, lifetime, or const generic: `T: Into<String>`,`'a: 'b`,`const LEN: usize`.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an impl block.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplRestriction.html)- Restriction - `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/enum.Item.html)- `full`
- Things that can appear directly inside of a module or scope.
- [Lit](https://docs.rs/enum.Lit.html)
- A Rust literal such as a string or integer or boolean.
- [Macro](https://docs.rs/enum.MacroDelimiter.html)- Delimiter - `derive`or- `full`
- A grouping token that surrounds a macro body: `m!(...)`or`m!{...}`or`m![...]`.
- [Member](https://docs.rs/enum.Member.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A struct or tuple struct field accessed in a struct literal or field expression.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/enum.Meta.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Content of a compile-time structured attribute.
- [Pat](https://docs.rs/enum.Pat.html)- `full`
- A pattern in a local binding, function signature, match expression, or various other places.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/enum.PathArguments.html)- Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed or parenthesized arguments of a path segment.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/enum.PointerMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- Mutability of a raw pointer (`*const T`,`*mut T`), in which non-mutable isn’t the implicit default.
- [Range](https://docs.rs/enum.RangeLimits.html)- Limits - `full`
- Limit types of a range, inclusive or exclusive.
- [Return](https://docs.rs/enum.ReturnType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- Return type of a function signature.
- [Static](https://docs.rs/enum.StaticMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- The mutability of an `Item::Static`or`ForeignItem::Static`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)- `full`
- A statement, usually ending in a semicolon.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitBoundModifier.html)- Bound - Modifier - `derive`or- `full`
- A modifier on a trait bound, currently only used for the `?`in`?Sized`.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item declaration within the definition of a trait.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The possible types that a Rust value could have.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeParamBound.html)- Param - Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait or lifetime used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [UnOp](https://docs.rs/enum.UnOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A unary operator: `*`,`!`,`-`.
- [UseTree](https://docs.rs/enum.UseTree.html)- `full`
- A suffix of an import tree in a `use`item:`Type as Renamed`or`*`.
- [Visibility](https://docs.rs/enum.Visibility.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The visibility level of an item: inherited or `pub`or`pub(restricted)`.
- [Where](https://docs.rs/enum.WherePredicate.html)- Predicate - `derive`or- `full`
- A single predicate in a `where`clause:`T: Deserialize<'de>`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)- `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse tokens of source code into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse2](https://docs.rs/fn.parse2.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a proc-macro2 token stream into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_file.html)- file - `full`and- `parsing`
- Parse the content of a file of Rust code.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_str.html)- str - `parsing`
- Parse a string of Rust code into the chosen syntax tree node.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- The result of a Syn parser.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/index.html

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

# quote_spanned in quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/1.0.45/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quote/macro.quote_spanned.html

```
macro_rules! quote_spanned {
    ($span:expr=> $($tt:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within
the macro invocation.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

A span expression of type [ Span](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/proc_macro2/struct.Span.html), followed by

`=>`, followed by the tokens
to quote. The span expression should be brief — use a variable for
anything more than a few characters. There should be no space before the
`=>` token.```
let span = /* ... */;
// On one line, use parentheses.
let tokens = quote_spanned!(span=> Box::into_raw(Box::new(#init)));
// On multiple lines, place the span at the top and use braces.
let tokens = quote_spanned! {span=>
    Box::into_raw(Box::new(#init))
};
```
The lack of space before the `=>` should look jarring to Rust programmers
and this is intentional. The formatting is designed to be visibly
off-balance and draw the eye a particular way, due to the span expression
being evaluated in the context of the procedural macro and the remaining
tokens being evaluated in the generated code.

[§](https://docs.rs#hygiene)Hygiene

Any interpolated tokens preserve the `Span` information provided by their
`ToTokens` implementation. Tokens that originate within the `quote_spanned!`
invocation are spanned with the given span argument.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following procedural macro code uses `quote_spanned!` to assert that a
particular Rust type implements the [ Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) trait so that references can be
safely shared between threads.

```
let ty_span = ty.span();
let assert_sync = quote_spanned! {ty_span=>
    struct _AssertSync where #ty: Sync;
};
```
If the assertion fails, the user will see an error like the following. The input span of their type is highlighted in the error.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `*const (): std::marker::Sync` is not satisfied
  --> src/main.rs:10:21
   |
10 |     static ref PTR: *const () = &();
   |                     ^^^^^^^^^ `*const ()` cannot be shared between threads safely
```
In this example it is important for the where-clause to be spanned with the line/column information of the user’s input type so that error messages are placed appropriately by the compiler.

# ccr 0.2.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ccr/0.2.4

## What it does

Scans every supported tool's session store, ranks each session by last activity, and resumes the one you pick — in its original working directory, with its original session ID, via the right CLI.

Each row's subtitle is the **last** user message in that session, so you see
what you were working on most recently — not how the chat opened. Press `n`
on any row to add a yellow nickname; nicknamed rows expand to a third line
that keeps the auto-derived title visible (dim) for context, and the
nickname is searched by `/` too.

```
┌─ ccr — 211 sessions  (2 possibly live) ──────────────────────────────────┐
│ Sessions                              │ Preview                          │
│ ▶ [claude] api-service        12m ago │ nick:    panic hotfix            │
│     panic hotfix                      │ tool:    claude                  │
│     actually let's also add a regr…   │ cwd:     ~/projects/api-service  │
│   [codex]  web-app         1h ● live  │ last:    2026-05-23 14:00  (12m) │
│     use exponential backoff capped…   │ msgs:    47                      │
│   [gemini] cli-tool             3d    │ id:      a1b2c3d4-5e6f-…         │
│     update the migration guide se…    │                                  │
│   [claude] docs-site            1w    │ ── recent turns ──               │
│     tighten the intro paragraph a…    │ ❯ user                           │
│                                       │ the panic reproduces only when…  │
│                                       │ ◆ asst                           │
│                                       │ Let me add a None check in the…  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ↑↓/jk · Enter resume · b bookmark · n nickname · / filter · ? help · q
```
Top row is **nicknamed** — `panic hotfix` shows in yellow, the auto-derived
last-message title stays visible underneath in dim gray. Rows without a
nickname are two lines (tags + auto-title), the same as before.

If a selected session is already running elsewhere (detected via `pgrep`,
matching only processes that carry the id as a resume argument —
`--resume <id>` / `-r <id>` / `resume <id>`), a confirmation modal appears before spawning
a second attachment:

```
        ┌─ Confirm resume ──────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ ⚠  Session may already be running                     │
        │                                                       │
        │ tool:    claude                                       │
        │ session: a1b2c3d4-5e6f-7890-abcd-…                    │
        │ cwd:     ~/projects/web-app                           │
        │                                                       │
        │ matching processes:                                   │
        │ 42318 claude --resume a1b2c3d4-5e6f-…                 │
        │                                                       │
        │ Resuming may interleave writes and corrupt session.   │
        │                                                       │
        │ [y] resume anyway    [n] cancel                       │
        └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
## Install

```
```
Or from source:

```
```
## Use

```
```
| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `↑`/`k` | up |
| `↓`/`j` | down |
| `g`/`Home` | jump to top |
| `G`/`End` | jump to bottom |
| `PgUp/Dn` | page up/down (10 rows) |
| `/` | filter: title, cwd, tool, nickname, or content (recent turns only) |
| `Enter` | resume selected session (live-checked) |
| `v` | open session in [agx](https://github.com/brevity1swos/agx)(timeline viewer) |
| `b` | toggle bookmark (★ marker, persisted) |
| `n` | set / edit / clear session nickname (yellow label) |
| `?`/`F1` | help overlay |
| `q`/`Esc` | quit |

On `Enter`, `ccr` runs a live-check first: `pgrep` prefilters processes that
mention the id, then only those carrying it as a resume argument
(`--resume <id>` / `-r <id>` / `resume <id>`, fused `--resume=<id>` too) count as live — an editor or
`tail -f` with the session file open does not. If a match is found, a
confirmation modal warns before spawning a second attachment (which would
interleave JSONL writes and corrupt the session). Otherwise it execs the
tool's resume command with the session's original `cwd`.

## CLI subcommands

| Command | Action |
|---|---|
| `ccr resume <id>` | resume a session directly by id, skipping the picker ( `--force`to override the live-session guard) |
| `ccr list` | plain-text dump of all sessions (tool id date title) |
| `ccr path <id>` | absolute path to session file (pipes well) |
| `ccr show <id>` | raw file contents (same as `cat $(ccr path <id>)`) |
| `ccr export <id>` | full-turn markdown dump (or `--format json`) |
| `ccr stats` | totals, per-tool, per-project, 30-day activity histogram |

`ccr resume <id>` runs the same live-check as the TUI: if the session looks
like it is already open elsewhere (a process carries the id as a resume
argument) it refuses, since a second attachment interleaves JSONL writes and
corrupts the session. Pass `--force` to resume anyway. The id is any id from
`ccr list`. On success the resumed tool's exit code is propagated; a refusal
or any error exits 1.

`ccr` never modifies your session files. If you want to delete one, delete
it where its tool stored it (`~/.claude/projects/...`, `~/.codex/sessions/...`,
or `~/.gemini/tmp/...`).

## Environment variables

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `CCR_CLAUDE_DIR` | Full path to Claude's `projects/`dir |
| `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | Claude Code's native override; `ccr`appends`projects` |
| `CCR_CODEX_DIR` | Full path to Codex's `sessions/`dir |
| `CCR_GEMINI_DIR` | Full path to Gemini's `~/.gemini`root |
| `CCR_BOOKMARKS_FILE` | Override the `~/.ccr/bookmarks.json`location |
| `CCR_NICKNAMES_FILE` | Override the `~/.ccr/nicknames.json`location |

## How it works

Each backend knows where its tool stores sessions and how to resume one.

| Tool | Storage | Resume invocation |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<uuid>.jsonl` | `claude --resume <uuid>`(cwd set) |
| Codex | `~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*.jsonl` | `codex resume <uuid>`(cwd set) |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/tmp/<project>/chats/session-*.json`+`projects.json` | `gemini --resume <N>`— ccr looks up the 1-based index at runtime via`gemini --list-sessions` |

For each session `ccr` extracts:

- `cwd`— working directory the session was started in
- title — **last**user message in the session, truncated to 80 chars (so the list shows what you were working on most recently, not how the chat opened)
- `last_activity`— most recent turn timestamp (drives the sort and the- `● live`flag)
- `message_count`— user + assistant turns only
- `preview`— last 6 turns, rendered in the right pane

Read-only at rest. `ccr` never touches your session files. The only state it
writes is `~/.ccr/bookmarks.json` (when you press `b`) and
`~/.ccr/nicknames.json` (when you press `n`). Both are plain JSON.

## Adding a backend

A backend is any type that implements:

```
```
Register it in `backends::all()` and sessions surface in the shared TUI with a
`[tool]` tag in the left column.

# toolport 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/toolport/0.1.0

# toolport

Companion CLI for [Toolport](https://toolport.app), the local gateway for your MCP servers.

Toolport is a desktop app that gives every AI client (Claude, Cursor, VS Code, and more)
one connection point for all your MCP servers, with **lazy tool discovery** that keeps the
standing tool-context cost roughly 99% smaller than loading every tool on every request.

This crate is a lightweight pointer - install it to print what Toolport is and where to get it:

```
```

# deepstrike_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/deepstrike-core/0.2.36/deepstrike_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#deepstrike-core)DeepStrike Core

Cross-language agent runtime kernel — pure computation, zero I/O.

This crate provides the core state machines, data structures, and algorithms for the DeepStrike agent framework. It is designed to be embedded via FFI bindings (PyO3, napi-rs, wasm-bindgen) into any language runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐
│ Python SDK  │  │ Node.js SDK │  │  WASM SDK   │
└──────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘
       └────────┬───────┴────────┬───────┘
                │  deepstrike-core │
                └─────────────────┘
```
[§](https://docs.rs#design-principles)Design Principles

- **Pure computation**: No I/O, no async, no network calls
- **State machine driven**: SDK feeds events, kernel returns actions
- **Zero-copy where possible**: CompactString, borrowed slices
- **Compile-time safety**: Ownership, Send+Sync, exhaustive matches

# awsm-renderer-scene-loader

Loads an `awsm-renderer-scene` runtime bundle (`scene.toml` + `assets/`) into the
renderer. The parallel to `awsm-renderer-gltf`'s `populate_gltf`: that loads
*foreign* glTF, this loads *our* format. They share the same renderer core — glb
meshes in a bundle go through `populate_gltf`'s machinery, primitives regenerate
via `awsm-renderer-meshgen`, and our materials / clips bind on top.

## What's here

- `populate_awsm_scene(renderer, scene, assets, on_phase)`— the entry point. Loads the node hierarchy (transforms), primitive + glb + skinned meshes, lights (with shadow params), cameras, textures, custom-WGSL materials, and animation clips + the NLA mixer. Returns a- `LoadedScene`of the inserted handles for later teardown.
- Submodules: `material`,`texture`,`dynamic`(custom-WGSL),`light`,`camera`,`animation`.

`assets` is an in-memory map of bundle-relative paths → bytes, so loading never
touches disk. `on_phase` reports each `LoadPhase` boundary (through pipeline
compile) for live progress; pass `|_| {}` to ignore it.

## Batched, phased load

The work runs as one phased pass, efficient for the player's typical "load a bundle then render" case:

- **Build materials**— lower every node's authored material and insert once, so meshes (including glb meshes via- `GltfMaterialSource::Single`) reference a ready key instead of letting the glTF loader mint a throwaway default.
- **Upload textures**— one batched- `finalize_gpu_textures`for the whole scene.
- **Upload meshes**— transforms + geometry (+ skins) + lights. The scene's animation clips + NLA mixer are then lowered against the per-node keys built in the prior phases (this step reports no separate- `LoadPhase`).
- **Compile pipelines**— one drive-to-ready for all materials + shadows, so the first frame draws everything rather than trickling pipelines across frames.

The headline consumer is the **round-trip test**: in the MCP-controlled browser
session, `export_player_bundle` → `populate_awsm_scene` → screenshot, compared
against the source render. The loader only LOADS clips; the consumer drives the
clock (a player's `update_animations`, or the editor round-trip's playhead pin).

## Companion crates

- `awsm-renderer-scene`— the runtime schema this loads.
- `awsm-renderer`/- `awsm-renderer-gltf`— the renderer core and the shared glTF upload path it reuses.

# ferridriver_bdd_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferridriver-bdd-macros/0.5.0/ferridriver_bdd_macros/

## Expand description

Proc macros for the ferridriver BDD/Cucumber framework.

Provides step definition macros that register async handler functions
via `inventory` for automatic collection at runtime.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ferridriver_bdd::prelude::*;
#[given("I navigate to {string}")]
async fn navigate(world: &mut BrowserWorld, url: String) {
    world.page().goto(&url, None).await.map_err(|e| step_err!("{e}"))?;
}
#[when("I click {string}")]
async fn click(world: &mut BrowserWorld, selector: String) {
    world.page().locator(&selector, None).click(None).await.map_err(|e| step_err!("{e}"))?;
}
#[then("the page title should be {string}")]
async fn check_title(world: &mut BrowserWorld, expected: String) {
    let title = world.page().title().await.map_err(|e| step_err!("{e}"))?;
    assert_eq!(title, expected);
}
```
## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [after](https://docs.rs/attr.after.html)
- Register an After hook.
- [before](https://docs.rs/attr.before.html)
- Register a Before hook.
- [given](https://docs.rs/attr.given.html)
- Register a Given step definition.
- [param_](https://docs.rs/attr.param_type.html)- type
- Register a custom parameter type for Cucumber expressions.
- [step](https://docs.rs/attr.step.html)
- Register a keyword-agnostic step definition (matches Given/When/Then).
- [then](https://docs.rs/attr.then.html)
- Register a Then step definition.
- [when](https://docs.rs/attr.when.html)
- Register a When step definition.

# ferridriver_test_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferridriver-test-macros/0.5.0/ferridriver_test_macros/

## Expand description

Proc macros for the ferridriver test framework.

Provides `#[ferritest]` to register async browser test functions. The
annotated function takes a single `TestContext`; built-in fixtures
(`page`, `browser`, `context`, …) resolve lazily through it.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ferridriver_test::prelude::*;
#[ferritest]
async fn basic_navigation(ctx: TestContext) {
    let page = ctx.page().await?;
    page.goto("https://example.com", None).await?;
    expect(&page).to_have_title("Example").await?;
}
#[ferritest(retries = 2, timeout = "30s", tag = "smoke")]
async fn flaky_test(ctx: TestContext) {
    let page = ctx.page().await?;
    let context = ctx.browser_context().await?;
    // ...
}
```
## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [after_](https://docs.rs/attr.after_all.html)- all
- Runs once after all tests in the containing module (suite).
- [after_](https://docs.rs/attr.after_each.html)- each
- Runs after each test in the containing module (suite), even on failure.
- [before_](https://docs.rs/attr.before_all.html)- all
- Runs once before all tests in the containing module (suite).
- [before_](https://docs.rs/attr.before_each.html)- each
- Runs before each test in the containing module (suite).
- [ferritest](https://docs.rs/attr.ferritest.html)
- `#[ferritest]`attribute macro.
- [ferritest_](https://docs.rs/attr.ferritest_each.html)- each
- `#[ferritest_each(data = [("a", 1), ("b", 2)])]`— parameterized test macro.
- [ferritest_](https://docs.rs/attr.ferritest_suite.html)- suite
- `#[ferritest_suite(mode = "serial")]`— set the execution mode of every- `#[ferritest]`in the annotated module. A serial suite is dispatched as one batch to a single worker, runs in source order, and skips the rest on first failure. The default (no attribute) is parallel.
- [fixture](https://docs.rs/attr.fixture.html)
- `#[fixture]`— register a custom, dependency-injected, scoped fixture.

# token_calibrator - Rust

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use calibrator::`- [TokenCalibratorOptions](https://docs.rs/calibrator/struct.TokenCalibratorOptions.html);
- `pub use estimator::`- [TokenEstimator](https://docs.rs/estimator/struct.TokenEstimator.html);
- `pub use estimator::`- [TokenEstimatorOptions](https://docs.rs/estimator/struct.TokenEstimatorOptions.html);
- `pub use builtin_rates::`- [BUILTIN_TOKEN_RATES](https://docs.rs/builtin_rates/static.BUILTIN_TOKEN_RATES.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buckets](https://docs.rs/buckets/index.html)
- Bucketing + pure estimation — the model-blind feature layer.
- [builtin_](https://docs.rs/builtin_rates/index.html)- rates
- Built-in per-model token rates (shipped baseline).
- [calibration](https://docs.rs/calibration/index.html)
- Calibration — the pure ridge-regression math that turns observed
(text, realTokens) rounds into per-bucket rates. Model-blind and stateless;
the stateful writer/reader wrappers live in `calibrator`/`estimator`.
- [calibrator](https://docs.rs/calibrator/index.html)
- TokenCalibrator (writer) — the stateful producer side. Wraps ONE model’s
data-only accumulator: feed it real usage via `observe`, read back solved`rates()`or the raw`to_matrix()`for persistence.
- [estimator](https://docs.rs/estimator/index.html)
- TokenEstimator (reader) — the stateful consumer side (renderer / CLI display).
Built from a `{model: matrix}`map; derives + caches each model’s rates up front. Pure math is in`calibration`; this is per-model lookup plus the shipped-baseline fallback.

---

# awsm_renderer_gltf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-gltf/0.12.0/awsm_renderer_gltf/

## Expand description

glTF ingestion for `awsm-renderer`.

Extracted from `awsm-renderer` as part of the editor-renderer overhaul.
glTF is one ingestion path into the renderer’s public raw-mesh API; it
is not privileged. Any other format (USD, custom, procedural) consumes
the same renderer surface this crate uses.

Loading flow:

- `loader::load_gltf`(async) fetches- `.gltf`/- `.glb`+ external buffers / images, parses into a- `GltfData`.
- `AwsmRenderer::populate_gltf(...)`(via the- `AwsmRendererGltfExt`extension trait below) walks the parsed scene and uploads meshes, materials, textures, animations, skins, transforms into the renderer.
- The caller gets back a `GltfKeyLookups`mapping per-document glTF indices to renderer keys (mesh / material / transform / animation).

# awsm_renderer_gltf_convert - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-gltf-convert/0.12.0/awsm_renderer_gltf_convert/

## Expand description

Pure-data glTF → canonical AWSM-format conversion.

This is the single import/convert path (see `docs/buffers.md`). It runs entirely on bytes — no GPU,
no browser, no renderer — so it’s exhaustively property-testable. Both the
editor and the player call [ convert](https://docs.rs/fn.convert.html) before any population:

```
foreign glTF ──convert──▶ self-contained canonical glb (geometry + materials
                          + textures, AWSM_format-stamped)
                          + extracted material / animation specs (for the bridge)
our own glb (AWSM_format) ──convert──▶ passed through unchanged
```
The [ AWSM_FORMAT](https://docs.rs/constant.AWSM_FORMAT.html) extension marker makes the round-trip idempotent:
converting our own export is a no-op (

`convert(convert(x)) == convert(x)`).[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-status-overnight-phase-3--see-the-plan-doc)Implementation status (overnight Phase 3 — see the plan doc)

Increment 1 (this file): crate + `AWSM_FORMAT` + detection + the geometry
conversion (clean glb via `glb-export`’s `reexport_clean_scene`/`write_glb`).
FOLLOW-ON increments, each its own commit:

- stamp `AWSM_FORMAT`onto the output glb (needs a`glb-export`writer hook) → unlocks the idempotency pass-through + its proptest;
- bake tangents + ensure normals into the canonical glb (needs
`MeshData.tangents`+ a`TANGENT`accessor in`glb-export::write_glb`);
- extract materials + animations (move the pure logic out of the editor
bridge: `extract_material_specs`/`extract_extensions`/`extract_animations`).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use animations::`- [extract_animations](https://docs.rs/animations/fn.extract_animations.html);
- `pub use animations::`- [AnimChannel](https://docs.rs/animations/struct.AnimChannel.html);
- `pub use animations::`- [AnimProperty](https://docs.rs/animations/enum.AnimProperty.html);
- `pub use animations::`- [AnimationSpec](https://docs.rs/animations/struct.AnimationSpec.html);
- `pub use animations::`- [Interpolation](https://docs.rs/animations/enum.Interpolation.html);
- `pub use images::`- [extract_images](https://docs.rs/images/fn.extract_images.html);
- `pub use images::`- [ImageData](https://docs.rs/images/struct.ImageData.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [extract_extensions](https://docs.rs/materials/fn.extract_extensions.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [extract_materials](https://docs.rs/materials/fn.extract_materials.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [AlphaMode](https://docs.rs/materials/enum.AlphaMode.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [Clearcoat](https://docs.rs/materials/struct.Clearcoat.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [animations](https://docs.rs/animations/index.html)
- Animation extraction — reads a source glTF’s animations into NEUTRAL specs
(raw sampler data: times + flattened output values + interpolation), keyed by
glTF node index. Pure glTF reading via the crate’s animation channel reader —
no renderer types (renderer-gltf’s `extract_animations`produces renderer`AnimationClip`s and so can’t live here). The editor/player map node_index → NodeId and lower the sampler into their own keyframes at the wiring step.
- [images](https://docs.rs/images/index.html)
- Texture-image extraction — pulls the RAW encoded image bytes (PNG/JPEG) out
of a glTF, indexed by glTF image index (the index `materials::TexRef.image`points at). Raw (not decoded) so the editor can write them straight to`assets/<id>.png`and the player decodes on GPU upload, same as it would from a bundle file. Pure data — no decode, no I/O.
- [materials](https://docs.rs/materials/index.html)
- Material extraction — reads a source glTF’s materials into NEUTRAL specs,
decoupled from both editor-protocol and scene types (each maps at its own
wiring step). Pure glTF reading; no GPU, no image upload (texture *image*bytes are pure data shipped separately; refs here point at glTF image indices).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Canonical](https://docs.rs/struct.CanonicalImport.html)- Import
- The result of `convert`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Convert](https://docs.rs/enum.ConvertError.html)- Error
- Conversion failures (all pure-data; no I/O).

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [AWSM_](https://docs.rs/constant.AWSM_FORMAT.html)- FORMAT
- Document-level glTF extension stamped onto a canonical AWSM glb. Its presence means “this glb was produced by our exporter / converter and is already in canonical form” — re-converting it is a no-op. Carries a version so a future canonical-form change is detectable rather than silently mis-read.
- [AWSM_](https://docs.rs/constant.AWSM_FORMAT_VERSION.html)- FORMAT_ - VERSION
- Current canonical-form version stamped under `AWSM_FORMAT``version`field.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [awsm_](https://docs.rs/fn.awsm_format_version.html)- format_ - version
- Read the `AWSM_format`version from an already-canonical document, if present.
- [convert](https://docs.rs/fn.convert.html)
- Normalize arbitrary glTF/GLB bytes to the canonical AWSM form.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_canonical.html)- canonical
- Does this parsed document carry the `AWSM_FORMAT`
- [stamp_](https://docs.rs/fn.stamp_awsm_format.html)- awsm_ - format
- Inject the `AWSM_FORMAT``extensionsUsed`and a document-level`extensions.AWSM_format = { version }`. Pure byte/JSON surgery on the JSON chunk (the BIN chunk is untouched), so the result re-parses as a normal glTF that`is_canonical`

# awsm_renderer_lod_bake - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-lod-bake/0.12.0/awsm_renderer_lod_bake/

## Expand description

`awsm-renderer-lod-bake` — offline LOD bake over plain geometry arrays.

Pure Rust, no GPU, **wasm-safe** (the bake runs inside the editor frontend,
a `wasm32-unknown-unknown` crate, so a C simplifier like meshoptimizer is not
an option — Apple clang has no wasm target). The shared primitive is a
boundary-locked half-edge QEM collapse ([`simplify`]) that keeps the
surviving vertices a *subset* of the originals, so per-vertex attributes
(skin weights, morph deltas, …) carry through a level verbatim.

Phase A (discrete LOD chain) uses [ build_lod_chain](https://docs.rs/simplify/fn.build_lod_chain.html); Phase B (cluster LOD
DAG) will reuse the same collapse with locked group boundaries.
