## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [cluster](https://docs.rs/cluster/index.html)
- Cluster (meshlet) generation for the cluster-LOD DAG (Phase B).
- [cluster_](https://docs.rs/cluster_mesh/index.html)- mesh
- Serializable cluster-LOD bake output (Phase B, B.1d): a shared vertex buffer
plus per-cluster **index pages**and meta, ready to upload as GPU buffers and evaluate the LOD cut on-device (B.2/B.3).
- [dag](https://docs.rs/dag/index.html)
- Cluster LOD DAG build (Phase B, B.1c).
- [manifest](https://docs.rs/manifest/index.html)
- The per-mesh LOD descriptor written into the player bundle alongside the level geometry, and read back by the runtime to drive level selection.
- [plan](https://docs.rs/plan/index.html)
- Discrete LOD-chain planning: decide *which*levels to emit for a mesh and describe them, without touching any file format. The caller (the editor bake) turns each`PlannedLevel``LodPlan::manifest`
- [quadric](https://docs.rs/quadric/index.html)
- Symmetric 4×4 error quadric (Garland–Heckbert QEM), stored as its 10 unique
upper-triangular entries. All math is `f64`for numerical stability across many accumulated planes; callers cast the final error to`f32`.
- [simplify](https://docs.rs/simplify/index.html)
- Boundary-locked half-edge QEM simplification.

# awsm_renderer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer/0.12.0/awsm_renderer/

## Expand description

High-level renderer API and shared modules.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-scene-schema-feature-optional-schema--runtime-bridge)The `scene-schema` feature (optional schema → runtime bridge)

[ awsm-renderer-scene](https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-scene) is the pure-data,
on-disk authoring format (

`EditorProject`, saved as `project.json`). The
renderer holds the *runtime*equivalents of those types. Enabling the

`scene-schema` feature pulls in `awsm-renderer-scene` (an optional dep) and
compiles a set of `From<awsm_renderer_scene::*>` impls so a consumer can convert
authored data into renderer config with a single `.into()`:[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let project: awsm_renderer_scene::EditorProject = serde_json::from_str(&text)?;
renderer.set_shadows_config(project.shadows.into());
```
It is **off by default**: a bare runtime consumer never pays for the schema
crate, and the editor frontends keep their own bridges. It exists mainly for
standalone *players* that load `EditorProject` bundles and want first-party
conversion that lives next to the runtime structs (so it can never drift).

[§](https://docs.rs#adding-more-conversions)Adding more conversions

This is an **extension point**, not a one-off. Today the only bridge is
shadows (`shadows::schema_convert`, gated by `#[cfg(feature = "scene-schema")]`). To bridge another subsystem (environment, lights,
materials, …), add a feature-gated `schema_convert` module beside that
subsystem’s runtime types and write the `From` impls there, following
`shadows::schema_convert` as the template. Keeping each bridge next to the
structs it maps is what stops the conversions from rotting.

Re-fires on a cadence (frame 5, then every 30) — NOT one-shot — so the drawn cut is observable as the camera/scene change (Gap-B paging A2 + the A3 cut-vs-source numbers); the async handler logs only when the value changes (`last_value`, init`-1`).

When the resolved value is non-zero, the next render preamble calls`crate::AwsmRenderer::set_max_per_froxel_capacity``(current * 2)`so subsequent frames have headroom. Single-buffered (`inflight`gates the next kick).

- Coarse-grained stages the renderer passes through during

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [COMPATIBITLIY_](https://docs.rs/static.COMPATIBITLIY_REQUIREMENTS.html)- REQUIREMENTS
- Compatibility requirements for this renderer.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [edge_](https://docs.rs/fn.edge_resolve_supported.html)- resolve_ - supported
- Returns true if the device can host the Stage 3 / Priority 3 per-shader-id MSAA edge-resolve pipelines.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Renderer](https://docs.rs/type.RendererLoadingPhaseHandler.html)- Loading - Phase - Handler
- Boxed phase-transition callback handed to the builder via
`AwsmRendererBuilder::with_phase_handler``Send + Sync`.

# syn 2.0.118 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/syn/2.0.118

# Parser for Rust source code

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user's code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

## Resources

The best way to learn about procedural macros is by writing some. Consider
working through [this procedural macro workshop](https://github.com/dtolnay/proc-macro-workshop) to get familiar with
the different types of procedural macros. The workshop contains relevant links
into the Syn documentation as you work through each project.

## Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary Rust
function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of the trait
we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user's code, the Rust
compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We get to execute
arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those tokens, then hand some
tokens back to the compiler to compile into the user's crate.

```
[]
 = "2.0"
 = "1.0"
[]
 = true
```
```
use TokenStream;
use quote;
use ;
```
The [ heapsize](https://docs.rs/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation of a
derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an estimate
of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data structures
in their program.

```
```
## Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler's error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a procedural
macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in Syn are able to
trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `std::thread::Thread`
```
## Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://docs.rs/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed using
Syn's parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static!
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
## Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild) crate
to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors detected by
the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the macro. Such tests
help avoid regressions from later refactors that mistakenly make an error no
longer trigger or be less helpful than it used to be.

## Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro, run
`cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of your own
test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last argument is
the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust's new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

## Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Proc macro shim

Syn operates on the token representation provided by the [proc-macro2](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0/proc_macro2/) crate
from crates.io rather than using the compiler's built in proc-macro crate
directly. This enables code using Syn to execute outside of the context of a
procedural macro, such as in unit tests or build.rs, and we avoid needing
incompatible ecosystems for proc macros vs non-macro use cases.

In general all of your code should be written against proc-macro2 rather than
proc-macro. The one exception is in the signatures of procedural macro entry
points, which are required by the language to use `proc_macro::TokenStream`.

The proc-macro2 crate will automatically detect and use the compiler's data structures when a procedural macro is active.

---

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0.118/src/syn/lib.rs.html

# syn/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! [![github]](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn) [![crates-io]](https://crates.io/crates/syn) [![docs-rs]](crate)
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! [github]: https://img.shields.io/badge/github-8da0cb?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=github
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [crates-io]: https://img.shields.io/badge/crates.io-fc8d62?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=rust
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! [docs-rs]: https://img.shields.io/badge/docs.rs-66c2a5?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=docs.rs
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! <br>
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! tree of Rust source code.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! - **Data structures** — Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!   represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!   [`syn::File`] which represents a full source file, but there are other
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!   entry points that may be useful to procedural macros including
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!   [`syn::Item`], [`syn::Expr`] and [`syn::Type`].
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! - **Derives** — Of particular interest to derive macros is
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!   [`syn::DeriveInput`] which is any of the three legal input items to a
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!   derive macro. An example below shows using this type in a library that can
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!   derive implementations of a user-defined trait.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! - **Parsing** — Parsing in Syn is built around [parser functions] with the
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!   signature `fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!   by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!   custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!   involving any of our syntax tree types.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! - **Location information** — Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!   `Span` that tracks line and column information back to the source of that
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!   token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!   messages pointing to all the right places in the user's code. There is an
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!   example of this below.
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! - **Feature flags** — Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!   procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!   time for all the rest.
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! [`syn::File`]: File
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! [`syn::Item`]: Item
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! [`syn::Expr`]: Expr
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! [`syn::Type`]: Type
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! [`syn::DeriveInput`]: DeriveInput
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! [parser functions]: mod@parse
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! <br>
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! # Example of a derive macro
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user's code,
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! user's crate.
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! [`TokenStream`]: proc_macro::TokenStream
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! ```toml
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! [dependencies]
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! syn = "2.0"
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! quote = "1.0"
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! [lib]
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! proc-macro = true
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! ```
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! ```
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! # extern crate proc_macro;
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! #
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! use proc_macro::TokenStream;
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! use quote::quote;
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! # const IGNORE_TOKENS: &str = stringify! {
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! #[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! # };
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!     // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!     let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     let expanded = quote! {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!         // ...
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!     };
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     TokenStream::from(expanded)
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! }
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! ```
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! The [`heapsize`] example directory shows a complete working implementation
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! of a derive macro. The example derives a `HeapSize` trait which computes an
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! [`heapsize`]: https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! ```
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! pub trait HeapSize {
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!     /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!     fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! }
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! ```
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! structures in their program.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! ```
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! # const IGNORE_TOKENS: &str = stringify! {
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! #[derive(HeapSize)]
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! # };
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!     a: Box<T>,
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!     b: u8,
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!     c: &'a str,
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!     d: String,
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! }
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! ```
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! <p><br></p>
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! # Spans and error reporting
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! compiler's error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! ```
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! # const IGNORE_TOKENS: &str = stringify! {
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! #[derive(HeapSize)]
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! # };
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! struct Broken {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!     ok: String,
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!     bad: std::thread::Thread,
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! }
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! ```
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! problem.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! ```text
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!  --> src/main.rs:7:5
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!   |
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! 7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! ```
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! <br>
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! # Parsing a custom syntax
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! The [`lazy-static`] example directory shows the implementation of a
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! `functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! using Syn's parsing API.
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! [`lazy-static`]: https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! procedural macro.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! ```
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! # macro_rules! lazy_static {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! #     ($($tt:tt)*) => {}
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! # }
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! #
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! lazy_static! {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!     static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! }
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! ```
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! on the macro input.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! ```text
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! warning: come on, pick a more creative name
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!   --> src/main.rs:10:16
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!    |
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! 10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!    |                ^^^
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! ```
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! <br>
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! # Testing
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [`trybuild`]
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! to be.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//!
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! [`trybuild`]: https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! <br>
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! # Debugging
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [`cargo expand`] subcommand.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//!
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! [`cargo expand`]: https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//!
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! [Debugging Rust's new Custom Derive system][debugging].
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! [debugging]: https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! <br>
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! # Optional features
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! are available.
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! - **`derive`** *(enabled by default)* — Data structures for representing the
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!   possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! - **`full`** — Data structures for representing the syntax tree of all valid
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!   Rust source code, including items and expressions.
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! - **`parsing`** *(enabled by default)* — Ability to parse input tokens into
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!   a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! - **`printing`** *(enabled by default)* — Ability to print a syntax tree
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!   node as tokens of Rust source code.
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! - **`visit`** — Trait for traversing a syntax tree.
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! - **`visit-mut`** — Trait for traversing and mutating in place a syntax
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!   tree.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! - **`fold`** — Trait for transforming an owned syntax tree.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! - **`clone-impls`** *(enabled by default)* — Clone impls for all syntax tree
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//!   types.
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! - **`extra-traits`** — Debug, Eq, PartialEq, Hash impls for all syntax tree
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!   types.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! - **`proc-macro`** *(enabled by default)* — Runtime dependency on the
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!   dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.
[250](https://docs.rs#250)

[553](https://docs.rs#553)mod [whitespace](https://docs.rs/whitespace.rs.html#1-65);
[554](https://docs.rs#554)
[555](https://docs.rs#555)#[rustfmt::skip] // https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/6176
[556](https://docs.rs#556)mod gen {
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    /// Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    ///
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    /// Each method of the [`Fold`] trait is a hook that can be overridden to
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    /// customize the behavior when transforming the corresponding type of node.
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    /// By default, every method recursively visits the substructure of the
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    /// input by invoking the right visitor method of each of its fields.
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    ///
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    /// [`Fold`]: fold::Fold
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    ///
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    /// ```
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    /// # use syn::{Attribute, BinOp, Expr, ExprBinary};
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    /// #
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    /// pub trait Fold {
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    ///     /* ... */
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    ///
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    ///     fn fold_expr_binary(&mut self, node: ExprBinary) -> ExprBinary {
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    ///         fold_expr_binary(self, node)
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    ///     }
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    ///
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    ///     /* ... */
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    ///     # fn fold_attribute(&mut self, node: Attribute) -> Attribute;
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    ///     # fn fold_expr(&mut self, node: Expr) -> Expr;
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    ///     # fn fold_bin_op(&mut self, node: BinOp) -> BinOp;
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// }
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    ///
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    /// pub fn fold_expr_binary<V>(v: &mut V, node: ExprBinary) -> ExprBinary
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// where
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    ///     V: Fold + ?Sized,
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    /// {
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    ///     ExprBinary {
[587](https://docs.rs#587)    ///         attrs: node
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    ///             .attrs
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    ///             .into_iter()
[590](https://docs.rs#590)    ///             .map(|attr| v.fold_attribute(attr))
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    ///             .collect(),
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    ///         left: Box::new(v.fold_expr(*node.left)),
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    ///         op: v.fold_bin_op(node.op),
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    ///         right: Box::new(v.fold_expr(*node.right)),
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    ///     }
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    /// }
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    ///
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    /// /* ... */
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    /// ```
[600](https://docs.rs#600)    ///
[601](https://docs.rs#601)    /// <br>
[602](https://docs.rs#602)    ///
[603](https://docs.rs#603)    /// # Example
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    ///
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    /// This fold inserts parentheses to fully parenthesizes any expression.
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    ///
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    /// ```
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    /// // [dependencies]
[609](https://docs.rs#609)    /// // quote = "1.0"
[610](https://docs.rs#610)    /// // syn = { version = "2.0", features = ["fold", "full"] }
[611](https://docs.rs#611)    ///
[612](https://docs.rs#612)    /// use quote::quote;
[613](https://docs.rs#613)    /// use syn::fold::{fold_expr, Fold};
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    /// use syn::{token, Expr, ExprParen};
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    ///
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    /// struct ParenthesizeEveryExpr;
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    ///
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    /// impl Fold for ParenthesizeEveryExpr {
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    ///     fn fold_expr(&mut self, expr: Expr) -> Expr {
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    ///         Expr::Paren(ExprParen {
[621](https://docs.rs#621)    ///             attrs: Vec::new(),
[622](https://docs.rs#622)    ///             expr: Box::new(fold_expr(self, expr)),
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    ///             paren_token: token::Paren::default(),
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    ///         })
[625](https://docs.rs#625)    ///     }
[626](https://docs.rs#626)    /// }
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    ///
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    /// fn main() {
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    ///     let code = quote! { a() + b(1) * c.d };
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    ///     let expr: Expr = syn::parse2(code).unwrap();
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    ///     let parenthesized = ParenthesizeEveryExpr.fold_expr(expr);
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    ///     println!("{}", quote!(#parenthesized));
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    ///
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    ///     // Output: (((a)()) + (((b)((1))) * ((c).d)))
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    /// }
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    /// ```
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    #[cfg(feature = "fold")]
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    #[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "fold")))]
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    #[rustfmt::skip]
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    pub mod [fold](https://docs.rs/gen/fold.rs.html#4-3906);
[641](https://docs.rs#641)
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    /// Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    ///
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    /// Each method of the [`Visit`] trait is a hook that can be overridden to
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// customize the behavior when visiting the corresponding type of node. By
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    /// default, every method recursively visits the substructure of the input
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    /// by invoking the right visitor method of each of its fields.
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    ///
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    /// [`Visit`]: visit::Visit
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    ///
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    /// ```
[652](https://docs.rs#652)    /// # use syn::{Attribute, BinOp, Expr, ExprBinary};
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    /// #
[654](https://docs.rs#654)    /// pub trait Visit<'ast> {
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    ///     /* ... */
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    ///
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    ///     fn visit_expr_binary(&mut self, node: &'ast ExprBinary) {
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    ///         visit_expr_binary(self, node);
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    ///     }
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    ///
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    ///     /* ... */
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    ///     # fn visit_attribute(&mut self, node: &'ast Attribute);
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    ///     # fn visit_expr(&mut self, node: &'ast Expr);
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    ///     # fn visit_bin_op(&mut self, node: &'ast BinOp);
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    /// }
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    ///
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    /// pub fn visit_expr_binary<'ast, V>(v: &mut V, node: &'ast ExprBinary)
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    /// where
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    ///     V: Visit<'ast> + ?Sized,
[670](https://docs.rs#670)    /// {
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    ///     for attr in &node.attrs {
[672](https://docs.rs#672)    ///         v.visit_attribute(attr);
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    ///     }
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    ///     v.visit_expr(&*node.left);
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    ///     v.visit_bin_op(&node.op);
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    ///     v.visit_expr(&*node.right);
[677](https://docs.rs#677)    /// }
[678](https://docs.rs#678)    ///
[679](https://docs.rs#679)    /// /* ... */
[680](https://docs.rs#680)    /// ```
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    ///
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    /// <br>
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    ///
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    /// # Example
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    ///
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// This visitor will print the name of every freestanding function in the
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    /// syntax tree, including nested functions.
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    ///
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// ```
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    /// // [dependencies]
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    /// // quote = "1.0"
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    /// // syn = { version = "2.0", features = ["full", "visit"] }
[693](https://docs.rs#693)    ///
[694](https://docs.rs#694)    /// use quote::quote;
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    /// use syn::visit::{self, Visit};
[696](https://docs.rs#696)    /// use syn::{File, ItemFn};
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    ///
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    /// struct FnVisitor;
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    ///
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    /// impl<'ast> Visit<'ast> for FnVisitor {
[701](https://docs.rs#701)    ///     fn visit_item_fn(&mut self, node: &'ast ItemFn) {
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    ///         println!("Function with name={}", node.sig.ident);
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    ///
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    ///         // Delegate to the default impl to visit any nested functions.
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    ///         visit::visit_item_fn(self, node);
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    ///     }
[707](https://docs.rs#707)    /// }
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    ///
[709](https://docs.rs#709)    /// fn main() {
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    ///     let code = quote! {
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    ///         pub fn f() {
[712](https://docs.rs#712)    ///             fn g() {}
[713](https://docs.rs#713)    ///         }
[714](https://docs.rs#714)    ///     };
[715](https://docs.rs#715)    ///
[716](https://docs.rs#716)    ///     let syntax_tree: File = syn::parse2(code).unwrap();
[717](https://docs.rs#717)    ///     FnVisitor.visit_file(&syntax_tree);
[718](https://docs.rs#718)    /// }
[719](https://docs.rs#719)    /// ```
[720](https://docs.rs#720)    ///
[721](https://docs.rs#721)    /// The `'ast` lifetime on the input references means that the syntax tree
[722](https://docs.rs#722)    /// outlives the complete recursive visit call, so the visitor is allowed to
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    /// hold on to references into the syntax tree.
[724](https://docs.rs#724)    ///
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    /// ```
[726](https://docs.rs#726)    /// use quote::quote;
[727](https://docs.rs#727)    /// use syn::visit::{self, Visit};
[728](https://docs.rs#728)    /// use syn::{File, ItemFn};
[729](https://docs.rs#729)    ///
[730](https://docs.rs#730)    /// struct FnVisitor<'ast> {
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    ///     functions: Vec<&'ast ItemFn>,
[732](https://docs.rs#732)    /// }
[733](https://docs.rs#733)    ///
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    /// impl<'ast> Visit<'ast> for FnVisitor<'ast> {
[735](https://docs.rs#735)    ///     fn visit_item_fn(&mut self, node: &'ast ItemFn) {
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    ///         self.functions.push(node);
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    ///         visit::visit_item_fn(self, node);
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    ///     }
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    /// }
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    ///
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    /// fn main() {
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    ///     let code = quote! {
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    ///         pub fn f() {
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    ///             fn g() {}
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    ///         }
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    ///     };
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    ///
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    ///     let syntax_tree: File = syn::parse2(code).unwrap();
[749](https://docs.rs#749)    ///     let mut visitor = FnVisitor { functions: Vec::new() };
[750](https://docs.rs#750)    ///     visitor.visit_file(&syntax_tree);
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    ///     for f in visitor.functions {
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    ///         println!("Function with name={}", f.sig.ident);
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    ///     }
[754](https://docs.rs#754)    /// }
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    /// ```
[756](https://docs.rs#756)    #[cfg(feature = "visit")]
[757](https://docs.rs#757)    #[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "visit")))]
[758](https://docs.rs#758)    #[rustfmt::skip]
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    pub mod [visit](https://docs.rs/gen/visit.rs.html#4-3941);
[760](https://docs.rs#760)
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    /// Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in
[762](https://docs.rs#762)    /// place.
[763](https://docs.rs#763)    ///
[764](https://docs.rs#764)    /// Each method of the [`VisitMut`] trait is a hook that can be overridden
[765](https://docs.rs#765)    /// to customize the behavior when mutating the corresponding type of node.
[766](https://docs.rs#766)    /// By default, every method recursively visits the substructure of the
[767](https://docs.rs#767)    /// input by invoking the right visitor method of each of its fields.
[768](https://docs.rs#768)    ///
[769](https://docs.rs#769)    /// [`VisitMut`]: visit_mut::VisitMut
[770](https://docs.rs#770)    ///
[771](https://docs.rs#771)    /// ```
[772](https://docs.rs#772)    /// # use syn::{Attribute, BinOp, Expr, ExprBinary};
[773](https://docs.rs#773)    /// #
[774](https://docs.rs#774)    /// pub trait VisitMut {
[775](https://docs.rs#775)    ///     /* ... */
[776](https://docs.rs#776)    ///
[777](https://docs.rs#777)    ///     fn visit_expr_binary_mut(&mut self, node: &mut ExprBinary) {
[778](https://docs.rs#778)    ///         visit_expr_binary_mut(self, node);
[779](https://docs.rs#779)    ///     }
[780](https://docs.rs#780)    ///
[781](https://docs.rs#781)    ///     /* ... */
[782](https://docs.rs#782)    ///     # fn visit_attribute_mut(&mut self, node: &mut Attribute);
[783](https://docs.rs#783)    ///     # fn visit_expr_mut(&mut self, node: &mut Expr);
[784](https://docs.rs#784)    ///     # fn visit_bin_op_mut(&mut self, node: &mut BinOp);
[785](https://docs.rs#785)    /// }
[786](https://docs.rs#786)    ///
[787](https://docs.rs#787)    /// pub fn visit_expr_binary_mut<V>(v: &mut V, node: &mut ExprBinary)
[788](https://docs.rs#788)    /// where
[789](https://docs.rs#789)    ///     V: VisitMut + ?Sized,
[790](https://docs.rs#790)    /// {
[791](https://docs.rs#791)    ///     for attr in &mut node.attrs {
[792](https://docs.rs#792)    ///         v.visit_attribute_mut(attr);
[793](https://docs.rs#793)    ///     }
[794](https://docs.rs#794)    ///     v.visit_expr_mut(&mut *node.left);
[795](https://docs.rs#795)    ///     v.visit_bin_op_mut(&mut node.op);
[796](https://docs.rs#796)    ///     v.visit_expr_mut(&mut *node.right);
[797](https://docs.rs#797)    /// }
[798](https://docs.rs#798)    ///
[799](https://docs.rs#799)    /// /* ... */
[800](https://docs.rs#800)    /// ```
[801](https://docs.rs#801)    ///
[802](https://docs.rs#802)    /// <br>
[803](https://docs.rs#803)    ///
[804](https://docs.rs#804)    /// # Example
[805](https://docs.rs#805)    ///
[806](https://docs.rs#806)    /// This mut visitor replace occurrences of u256 suffixed integer literals
[807](https://docs.rs#807)    /// like `999u256` with a macro invocation `bigint::u256!(999)`.
[808](https://docs.rs#808)    ///
[809](https://docs.rs#809)    /// ```
[810](https://docs.rs#810)    /// // [dependencies]
[811](https://docs.rs#811)    /// // quote = "1.0"
[812](https://docs.rs#812)    /// // syn = { version = "2.0", features = ["full", "visit-mut"] }
[813](https://docs.rs#813)    ///
[814](https://docs.rs#814)    /// use quote::quote;
[815](https://docs.rs#815)    /// use syn::visit_mut::{self, VisitMut};
[816](https://docs.rs#816)    /// use syn::{parse_quote, Expr, File, Lit, LitInt};
[817](https://docs.rs#817)    ///
[818](https://docs.rs#818)    /// struct BigintReplace;
[819](https://docs.rs#819)    ///
[820](https://docs.rs#820)    /// impl VisitMut for BigintReplace {
[821](https://docs.rs#821)    ///     fn visit_expr_mut(&mut self, node: &mut Expr) {
[822](https://docs.rs#822)    ///         if let Expr::Lit(expr) = &node {
[823](https://docs.rs#823)    ///             if let Lit::Int(int) = &expr.lit {
[824](https://docs.rs#824)    ///                 if int.suffix() == "u256" {
[825](https://docs.rs#825)    ///                     let digits = int.base10_digits();
[826](https://docs.rs#826)    ///                     let unsuffixed: LitInt = syn::parse_str(digits).unwrap();
[827](https://docs.rs#827)    ///                     *node = parse_quote!(bigint::u256!(#unsuffixed));
[828](https://docs.rs#828)    ///                     return;
[829](https://docs.rs#829)    ///                 }
[830](https://docs.rs#830)    ///             }
[831](https://docs.rs#831)    ///         }
[832](https://docs.rs#832)    ///
[833](https://docs.rs#833)    ///         // Delegate to the default impl to visit nested expressions.
[834](https://docs.rs#834)    ///         visit_mut::visit_expr_mut(self, node);
[835](https://docs.rs#835)    ///     }
[836](https://docs.rs#836)    /// }
[837](https://docs.rs#837)    ///
[838](https://docs.rs#838)    /// fn main() {
[839](https://docs.rs#839)    ///     let code = quote! {
[840](https://docs.rs#840)    ///         fn main() {
[841](https://docs.rs#841)    ///             let _ = 999u256;
[842](https://docs.rs#842)    ///         }
[843](https://docs.rs#843)    ///     };
[844](https://docs.rs#844)    ///
[845](https://docs.rs#845)    ///     let mut syntax_tree: File = syn::parse2(code).unwrap();
[846](https://docs.rs#846)    ///     BigintReplace.visit_file_mut(&mut syntax_tree);
[847](https://docs.rs#847)    ///     println!("{}", quote!(#syntax_tree));
[848](https://docs.rs#848)    /// }
[849](https://docs.rs#849)    /// ```
[850](https://docs.rs#850)    #[cfg(feature = "visit-mut")]
[851](https://docs.rs#851)    #[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "visit-mut")))]
[852](https://docs.rs#852)    #[rustfmt::skip]
[853](https://docs.rs#853)    pub mod [visit_mut](https://docs.rs/gen/visit_mut.rs.html#4-3761);
[854](https://docs.rs#854)
[855](https://docs.rs#855)    #[cfg(feature = "clone-impls")]
[856](https://docs.rs#856)    #[rustfmt::skip]
[857](https://docs.rs#857)    mod [clone](https://docs.rs/gen/clone.rs.html#4-2267);
[858](https://docs.rs#858)
[859](https://docs.rs#859)    #[cfg(feature = "extra-traits")]
[860](https://docs.rs#860)    #[rustfmt::skip]
[861](https://docs.rs#861)    mod [debug](https://docs.rs/gen/debug.rs.html#4-3238);
[862](https://docs.rs#862)
[863](https://docs.rs#863)    #[cfg(feature = "extra-traits")]
[864](https://docs.rs#864)    #[rustfmt::skip]
[865](https://docs.rs#865)    mod [eq](https://docs.rs/gen/eq.rs.html#4-2308);
[866](https://docs.rs#866)
[867](https://docs.rs#867)    #[cfg(feature = "extra-traits")]
[868](https://docs.rs#868)    #[rustfmt::skip]
[869](https://docs.rs#869)    mod [hash](https://docs.rs/gen/hash.rs.html#4-2878);

[889](https://docs.rs#889)#[cfg(all(feature = "parsing", feature = "full"))]
[890](https://docs.rs#890)use [alloc::string::ToString](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/string/trait.ToString.html);
[891](https://docs.rs#891)
[892](https://docs.rs#892)/// Parse tokens of source code into the chosen syntax tree node.
[893](https://docs.rs#893)///
[894](https://docs.rs#894)/// This is preferred over parsing a string because tokens are able to preserve
[895](https://docs.rs#895)/// information about where in the user's code they were originally written (the
[896](https://docs.rs#896)/// "span" of the token), possibly allowing the compiler to produce better error
[897](https://docs.rs#897)/// messages.
[898](https://docs.rs#898)///
[899](https://docs.rs#899)/// This function parses a `proc_macro::TokenStream` which is the type used for
[900](https://docs.rs#900)/// interop with the compiler in a procedural macro. To parse a
[901](https://docs.rs#901)/// `proc_macro2::TokenStream`, use [`syn::parse2`] instead.
[902](https://docs.rs#902)///
[903](https://docs.rs#903)/// [`syn::parse2`]: parse2
[904](https://docs.rs#904)///
[905](https://docs.rs#905)/// This function enforces that the input is fully parsed. If there are any
[906](https://docs.rs#906)/// unparsed tokens at the end of the stream, an error is returned.
[907](https://docs.rs#907)#[cfg(all(feature = "parsing", feature = "proc-macro"))]
[908](https://docs.rs#908)#[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(all(feature = "parsing", feature = "proc-macro"))))]
[909](https://docs.rs#909)pub fn [parse](https://docs.rs/syn/fn.parse.html)<T: [parse::Parse](https://docs.rs/parse.rs.html#215-217)>(tokens: proc_macro::[TokenStream](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/struct.TokenStream.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error.rs.html#19)<T> {
[910](https://docs.rs#910)    parse::Parser::[parse](https://docs.rs/parse.rs.html#1255-1257)(T::[parse](https://docs.rs/parse.rs.html#216), [tokens](https://docs.rs#909))
[911](https://docs.rs#911)}
[912](https://docs.rs#912)
[913](https://docs.rs#913)/// Parse a proc-macro2 token stream into the chosen syntax tree node.
[914](https://docs.rs#914)///
[915](https://docs.rs#915)/// This function parses a `proc_macro2::TokenStream` which is commonly useful
[916](https://docs.rs#916)/// when the input comes from a node of the Syn syntax tree, for example the
[917](https://docs.rs#917)/// body tokens of a [`Macro`] node. When in a procedural macro parsing the
[918](https://docs.rs#918)/// `proc_macro::TokenStream` provided by the compiler, use [`syn::parse`]
[919](https://docs.rs#919)/// instead.
[920](https://docs.rs#920)///
[921](https://docs.rs#921)/// [`syn::parse`]: parse()
[922](https://docs.rs#922)///
[923](https://docs.rs#923)/// This function enforces that the input is fully parsed. If there are any
[924](https://docs.rs#924)/// unparsed tokens at the end of the stream, an error is returned.
[925](https://docs.rs#925)#[cfg(feature = "parsing")]
[926](https://docs.rs#926)#[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "parsing")))]
[927](https://docs.rs#927)pub fn [parse2](https://docs.rs/syn/fn.parse2.html)<T: [parse::Parse](https://docs.rs/parse.rs.html#215-217)>(tokens: proc_macro2::[TokenStream](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/proc_macro2/struct.TokenStream.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error.rs.html#19)<T> {
[928](https://docs.rs#928)    parse::Parser::[parse2](https://docs.rs/parse.rs.html#1247)(T::[parse](https://docs.rs/parse.rs.html#216), [tokens](https://docs.rs#927))
[929](https://docs.rs#929)}
[930](https://docs.rs#930)
[931](https://docs.rs#931)/// Parse a string of Rust code into the chosen syntax tree node.
[932](https://docs.rs#932)///
[933](https://docs.rs#933)/// This function enforces that the input is fully parsed. If there are any
[934](https://docs.rs#934)/// unparsed tokens at the end of the stream, an error is returned.
[935](https://docs.rs#935)///
[936](https://docs.rs#936)/// # Hygiene
[937](https://docs.rs#937)///
[938](https://docs.rs#938)/// Every span in the resulting syntax tree will be set to resolve at the macro
[939](https://docs.rs#939)/// call site.
[940](https://docs.rs#940)///
[941](https://docs.rs#941)/// # Examples
[942](https://docs.rs#942)///
[943](https://docs.rs#943)/// ```
[944](https://docs.rs#944)/// use syn::{Expr, Result};
[945](https://docs.rs#945)///
[946](https://docs.rs#946)/// fn run() -> Result<()> {
[947](https://docs.rs#947)///     let code = "assert_eq!(u8::max_value(), 255)";
[948](https://docs.rs#948)///     let expr = syn::parse_str::<Expr>(code)?;
[949](https://docs.rs#949)///     println!("{:#?}", expr);
[950](https://docs.rs#950)///     Ok(())
[951](https://docs.rs#951)/// }
[952](https://docs.rs#952)/// #
[953](https://docs.rs#953)/// # run().unwrap();
[954](https://docs.rs#954)/// ```
[955](https://docs.rs#955)#[cfg(feature = "parsing")]
[956](https://docs.rs#956)#[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "parsing")))]
[957](https://docs.rs#957)pub fn [parse_str](https://docs.rs/syn/fn.parse_str.html)<T: [parse::Parse](https://docs.rs/parse.rs.html#215-217)>(s: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error.rs.html#19)<T> {
[958](https://docs.rs#958)    parse::Parser::[parse_str](https://docs.rs/parse.rs.html#1268-1270)(T::[parse](https://docs.rs/parse.rs.html#216), [s](https://docs.rs#957))
[959](https://docs.rs#959)}
[960](https://docs.rs#960)
[961](https://docs.rs#961)/// Parse the content of a file of Rust code.
[962](https://docs.rs#962)///
[963](https://docs.rs#963)/// This is different from `syn::parse_str::<File>(content)` in two ways:
[964](https://docs.rs#964)///
[965](https://docs.rs#965)/// - It discards a leading byte order mark `\u{FEFF}` if the file has one.
[966](https://docs.rs#966)/// - It preserves the shebang line of the file, such as `#!/usr/bin/env rustx`.
[967](https://docs.rs#967)///
[968](https://docs.rs#968)/// If present, either of these would be an error using `from_str`.
[969](https://docs.rs#969)///
[970](https://docs.rs#970)/// # Examples
[971](https://docs.rs#971)///
[972](https://docs.rs#972)/// ```no_run
[973](https://docs.rs#973)/// use std::error::Error;
[974](https://docs.rs#974)/// use std::fs;
[975](https://docs.rs#975)/// use std::io::Read;
[976](https://docs.rs#976)///
[977](https://docs.rs#977)/// fn run() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
[978](https://docs.rs#978)///     let content = fs::read_to_string("path/to/code.rs")?;
[979](https://docs.rs#979)///     let ast = syn::parse_file(&content)?;
[980](https://docs.rs#980)///     if let Some(shebang) = ast.shebang {
[981](https://docs.rs#981)///         println!("{}", shebang);
[982](https://docs.rs#982)///     }
[983](https://docs.rs#983)///     println!("{} items", ast.items.len());
[984](https://docs.rs#984)///
[985](https://docs.rs#985)///     Ok(())
[986](https://docs.rs#986)/// }
[987](https://docs.rs#987)/// #
[988](https://docs.rs#988)/// # run().unwrap();
[989](https://docs.rs#989)/// ```
[990](https://docs.rs#990)#[cfg(all(feature = "parsing", feature = "full"))]
[991](https://docs.rs#991)#[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(all(feature = "parsing", feature = "full"))))]
[992](https://docs.rs#992)pub fn [parse_file](https://docs.rs/syn/fn.parse_file.html)(mut content: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error.rs.html#19)<[File](https://docs.rs/file.rs.html#6-86)> {
[993](https://docs.rs#993)    // Strip the BOM if it is present
[994](https://docs.rs#994)    const BOM: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html) = "\u{feff}";
[995](https://docs.rs#995)    if [content](https://docs.rs#992).[starts_with](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/primitive.str.html#method.starts_with)([BOM](https://docs.rs#994)) {
[996](https://docs.rs#996)        [content](https://docs.rs#992) = &[content](https://docs.rs#992)[BOM.len()..];
[997](https://docs.rs#997)    }
[998](https://docs.rs#998)
[999](https://docs.rs#999)    let mut shebang = [None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/Option/variant.None.html);
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)    if [content](https://docs.rs#992).[starts_with](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/primitive.str.html#method.starts_with)("#!") {
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)        let rest = whitespace::[skip](https://docs.rs/whitespace.rs.html#1-60)(&[content](https://docs.rs#992)[2..]);
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)        if ![rest](https://docs.rs#1001).[starts_with](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/primitive.str.html#method.starts_with)('[') {
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)            if let [Some](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/Option/variant.Some.html)(idx) = [content](https://docs.rs#992).[find](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/primitive.str.html#method.find)('\n') {

`derive` or `full`## Expand description

A Rust expression.

*This type is available only if Syn is built with the  "derive" or "full"
feature, but most of the variants are not available unless “full” is enabled.*

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax-tree-enums)Syntax tree enums

This type is a syntax tree enum. In Syn this and other syntax tree enums are designed to be traversed using the following rebinding idiom.

```
let expr: Expr = /* ... */;
match expr {
    Expr::MethodCall(expr) => {
        /* ... */
    }
    Expr::Cast(expr) => {
        /* ... */
    }
    Expr::If(expr) => {
        /* ... */
    }
    /* ... */
```
We begin with a variable `expr` of type `Expr` that has no fields
(because it is an enum), and by matching on it and rebinding a variable
with the same name `expr` we effectively imbue our variable with all of
the data fields provided by the variant that it turned out to be. So for
example above if we ended up in the `MethodCall` case then we get to use
`expr.receiver`, `expr.args` etc; if we ended up in the `If` case we get
to use `expr.cond`, `expr.then_branch`, `expr.else_branch`.

This approach avoids repeating the variant names twice on every line.

```
// Repetitive; recommend not doing this.
match expr {
    Expr::MethodCall(ExprMethodCall { method, args, .. }) => {
```
In general, the name to which a syntax tree enum variant is bound should be a suitable name for the complete syntax tree enum type.

```
// Binding is called `base` which is the name I would use if I were
// assigning `*discriminant.base` without an `if let`.
if let Expr::Tuple(base) = *discriminant.base {
```
A sign that you may not be choosing the right variable names is if you
see names getting repeated in your code, like accessing
`receiver.receiver` or `pat.pat` or `cond.cond`.

#### pub const [PLACEHOLDER](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.PLACEHOLDER): Self

An unspecified invalid expression.

```
use core::mem;
use quote::ToTokens;
use syn::{parse_quote, Expr};
fn unparenthesize(e: &mut Expr) {
    while let Expr::Paren(paren) = e {
        *e = mem::replace(&mut *paren.expr, Expr::PLACEHOLDER);
    }
}
fn main() {
    let mut e: Expr = parse_quote! { ((1 + 1)) };
    unparenthesize(&mut e);
    assert_eq!("1 + 1", e.to_token_stream().to_string());
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#830-832)#### pub fn [parse_without_eager_brace](https://docs.rs#method.parse_without_eager_brace)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)>

**crate features **`full` and `parsing` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#830-832)

#### pub fn [parse_without_eager_brace](https://docs.rs#method.parse_without_eager_brace)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)>

**crate features**only.

`full` and `parsing`An alternative to the primary `Expr::parse` parser (from the [ Parse](https://docs.rs/parse/trait.Parse.html)
trait) for ambiguous syntactic positions in which a trailing brace
should not be taken as part of the expression.

Rust grammar has an ambiguity where braces sometimes turn a path
expression into a struct initialization and sometimes do not. In the
following code, the expression `S {}` is one expression. Presumably
there is an empty struct `struct S {}` defined somewhere which it is
instantiating.

```
let _ = *S {};
// parsed by rustc as: `*(S {})`
```
We would want to parse the above using `Expr::parse` after the `=`
token.

But in the following, `S {}` is *not* a struct init expression.

```
if *S {} {}
// parsed by rustc as:
//
//    if (*S) {
//        /* empty block */
//    }
//    {
//        /* another empty block */
//    }
```
For that reason we would want to parse if-conditions using
`Expr::parse_without_eager_brace` after the `if` token. Same for similar
syntactic positions such as the condition expr after a `while` token or
the expr at the top of a `match`.

The Rust grammar’s choices around which way this ambiguity is resolved at various syntactic positions is fairly arbitrary. Really either parse behavior could work in most positions, and language designers just decide each case based on which is more likely to be what the programmer had in mind most of the time.

```
if return S {} {}
// parsed by rustc as:
//
//    if (return (S {})) {
//    }
//
// but could equally well have been this other arbitrary choice:
//
//    if (return S) {
//    }
//    {}
```
Note the grammar ambiguity on trailing braces is distinct from
precedence and is not captured by assigning a precedence level to the
braced struct init expr in relation to other operators. This can be
illustrated by `return 0..S {}` vs `match 0..S {}`. The former parses as
`return (0..(S {}))` implying tighter precedence for struct init than
`..`, while the latter parses as `match (0..S) {}` implying tighter
precedence for `..` than struct init, a contradiction.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#892-894)#### pub fn [parse_with_earlier_boundary_rule](https://docs.rs#method.parse_with_earlier_boundary_rule)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)>

**crate features **`full` and `parsing` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#892-894)

#### pub fn [parse_with_earlier_boundary_rule](https://docs.rs#method.parse_with_earlier_boundary_rule)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)>

**crate features**only.

`full` and `parsing`An alternative to the primary `Expr::parse` parser (from the [ Parse](https://docs.rs/parse/trait.Parse.html)
trait) for syntactic positions in which expression boundaries are placed
more eagerly than done by the typical expression grammar. This includes
expressions at the head of a statement or in the right-hand side of a

`match` arm.Compare the following cases:

```
let _ = match result {
    () if guard => if cond { f } else { g }
    () => false,
};
```
```
let _ = || {
    if cond { f } else { g }
    ()
};
```
`let _ = [if cond { f } else { g } ()];`The same sequence of tokens `if cond { f } else { g } ()` appears in
expression position 3 times. The first two syntactic positions use eager
placement of expression boundaries, and parse as `Expr::If`, with the
adjacent `()` becoming `Pat::Tuple` or `Expr::Tuple`. In contrast, the
third case uses standard expression boundaries and parses as
`Expr::Call`.

As with [ parse_without_eager_brace](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html#method.parse_without_eager_brace), this ambiguity in the Rust
grammar is independent of precedence.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#908-924)#### pub fn [peek](https://docs.rs#method.peek)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

**crate feature **`parsing` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#908-924)

#### pub fn [peek](https://docs.rs#method.peek)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

**crate feature**only.

`parsing`Returns whether the next token in the parse stream is one that might possibly form the beginning of an expr.

This classification is a load-bearing part of the grammar of some Rust
expressions, notably `return` and `break`. For example `return < …` will
never parse `<` as a binary operator regardless of what comes after,
because `<` is a legal starting token for an expression and so it’s
required to be continued as a return value, such as `return <Struct as Trait>::CONST`. Meanwhile `return > …` treats the `>` as a binary
operator because it cannot be a starting token for any Rust expression.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

**crate feature**only.

# syn::parse - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0.118/syn/parse/index.html

**crate feature**only.

`parsing`## Expand description

Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.

Parsing in Syn is built on parser functions that take in a [ ParseStream](https://docs.rs/type.ParseStream.html)
and produce a

[where](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

`Result<T>``T` is some syntax tree node. Underlying
these parser functions is a lower level mechanism built around the
[type.](https://docs.rs/buffer/struct.Cursor.html)

`Cursor``Cursor` is a cheaply copyable cursor over a range of
tokens in a token stream.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Here is a snippet of parsing code to get a feel for the style of the
library. We define data structures for a subset of Rust syntax including
enums (not shown) and structs, then provide implementations of the [ Parse](https://docs.rs/trait.Parse.html)
trait to parse these syntax tree data structures from a token stream.

Once `Parse` impls have been defined, they can be called conveniently from a
procedural macro through [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html) as shown at the bottom of
the snippet. If the caller provides syntactically invalid input to the
procedural macro, they will receive a helpful compiler error message
pointing out the exact token that triggered the failure to parse.

```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use syn::{braced, parse_macro_input, token, Field, Ident, Result, Token};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream};
use syn::punctuated::Punctuated;
enum Item {
    Struct(ItemStruct),
    Enum(ItemEnum),
}
struct ItemStruct {
    struct_token: Token![struct],
    ident: Ident,
    brace_token: token::Brace,
    fields: Punctuated<Field, Token![,]>,
}
impl Parse for Item {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        let lookahead = input.lookahead1();
        if lookahead.peek(Token![struct]) {
            input.parse().map(Item::Struct)
        } else if lookahead.peek(Token![enum]) {
            input.parse().map(Item::Enum)
        } else {
            Err(lookahead.error())
        }
    }
}
impl Parse for ItemStruct {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        let content;
        Ok(ItemStruct {
            struct_token: input.parse()?,
            ident: input.parse()?,
            brace_token: braced!(content in input),
            fields: content.parse_terminated(Field::parse_named, Token![,])?,
        })
    }
}
#[proc_macro]
pub fn my_macro(tokens: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let input = parse_macro_input!(tokens as Item);
    /* ... */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-synparse-functions)The `syn::parse*` functions

The [ syn::parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/fn.parse2.html)

`syn::parse2`[functions serve as an entry point for parsing syntax tree nodes that can be parsed in an obvious default way. These functions can return any syntax tree node that implements the](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_str.html)

`syn::parse_str`[trait, which includes most types in Syn.](https://docs.rs/trait.Parse.html)

`Parse````
use syn::Type;
let t: Type = syn::parse_str("alloc::collections::HashMap<String, Value>")?;
```
The [ parse_quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html) macro also uses this approach.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-parser-trait)The `Parser` trait

Some types can be parsed in several ways depending on context. For example
an [ Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.Attribute.html) can be either “outer” like

`#[...]` or “inner” like
`#![...]` and parsing the wrong one would be a bug. Similarly [may or may not allow trailing punctuation, and parsing it the wrong way would either reject valid input or accept invalid input.](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)

`Punctuated`The `Parse` trait is not implemented in these cases because there is no good
behavior to consider the default.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Can't parse `Punctuated` without knowing whether trailing punctuation
// should be allowed in this context.
let path: Punctuated<PathSegment, Token![::]> = syn::parse(tokens)?;
```
In these cases the types provide a choice of parser functions rather than a
single `Parse` implementation, and those parser functions can be invoked
through the [ Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html) trait.

```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use syn::parse::Parser;
use syn::punctuated::Punctuated;
use syn::{Attribute, Expr, PathSegment, Result, Token};
fn call_some_parser_methods(input: TokenStream) -> Result<()> {
    // Parse a nonempty sequence of path segments separated by `::` punctuation
    // with no trailing punctuation.
    let tokens = input.clone();
    let parser = Punctuated::<PathSegment, Token![::]>::parse_separated_nonempty;
    let _path = parser.parse(tokens)?;
    // Parse a possibly empty sequence of expressions terminated by commas with
    // an optional trailing punctuation.
    let tokens = input.clone();
    let parser = Punctuated::<Expr, Token![,]>::parse_terminated;
    let _args = parser.parse(tokens)?;
    // Parse zero or more outer attributes but not inner attributes.
    let tokens = input.clone();
    let parser = Attribute::parse_outer;
    let _attrs = parser.parse(tokens)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [discouraged](https://docs.rs/discouraged/index.html)
- Extensions to the parsing API with niche applicability.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [End](https://docs.rs/struct.End.html)
- Pseudo-token used for peeking the end of a parse stream.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error returned when a Syn parser cannot parse the input tokens.
- [Lookahead1](https://docs.rs/struct.Lookahead1.html)
- Support for checking the next token in a stream to decide how to parse.
- [Nothing](https://docs.rs/struct.Nothing.html)
- An empty syntax tree node that consumes no tokens when parsed.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseBuffer.html)- Buffer
- Cursor position within a buffered token stream.
- [Step](https://docs.rs/struct.StepCursor.html)- Cursor
- Cursor state associated with speculative parsing.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Parse](https://docs.rs/trait.Parse.html)
- Parsing interface implemented by all types that can be parsed in a default way from a token stream.
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- Parser that can parse Rust tokens into a particular syntax tree node.
- [Peek](https://docs.rs/trait.Peek.html)
- Types that can be parsed by looking at just one token.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Parse](https://docs.rs/type.ParseStream.html)- Stream
- Input to a Syn parser function.
- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- The result of a Syn parser.

# syn::spanned - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0.118/syn/spanned/index.html

**crate features**only.

`parsing` and `printing`## Expand description

A trait that can provide the `Span` of the complete contents of a syntax
tree node.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Suppose in a procedural macro we have a [ Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html) that we want to assert
implements the

[trait. Maybe this is the type of one of the fields of a struct for which we are deriving a trait implementation, and we need to be able to pass a reference to one of those fields across threads.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sync.html)

`Sync`If the field type does *not* implement `Sync` as required, we want the
compiler to report an error pointing out exactly which type it was.

The following macro code takes a variable `ty` of type `Type` and produces a
static assertion that `Sync` is implemented for that type.

```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use proc_macro2::Span;
use quote::quote_spanned;
use syn::Type;
use syn::spanned::Spanned;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    /* ... */
    let assert_sync = quote_spanned! {ty.span()=>
        struct _AssertSync where #ty: Sync;
    };
    /* ... */
}
```
By inserting this `assert_sync` fragment into the output code generated by
our macro, the user’s code will fail to compile if `ty` does not implement
`Sync`. The errors they would see look like the following.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `*const i32: core::marker::Sync` is not satisfied
  --> src/main.rs:10:21
   |
10 |     bad_field: *const i32,
   |                ^^^^^^^^^^ `*const i32` cannot be shared between threads safely
```
In this technique, using the `Type`’s span for the error message makes the
error appear in the correct place underlining the right type.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

The underlying [ proc_macro::Span::join](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/struct.Span.html#method.join) method is nightly-only. When
called from within a procedural macro in a nightly compiler,

`Spanned` will
use `join` to produce the intended span. When not using a nightly compiler,
only the span of the *first token*of the syntax tree node is returned.

In the common case of wanting to use the joined span as the span of a
`syn::Error`, consider instead using [ syn::Error::new_spanned](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html#method.new_spanned) which is
able to span the error correctly under the complete syntax tree node without
needing the unstable

`join`.## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Spanned](https://docs.rs/trait.Spanned.html)
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.

---

# syn::token - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0.118/syn/token/index.html

## Expand description

Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.

The type names in this module can be difficult to keep straight, so we
prefer to use the [ Token!](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html) macro instead. This is a type-macro that
expands to the token type of the given token.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The [ ItemStatic](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemStatic.html) syntax tree node is defined like this.

```
pub struct ItemStatic {
    pub attrs: Vec<Attribute>,
    pub vis: Visibility,
    pub static_token: Token![static],
    pub mutability: Option<Token![mut]>,
    pub ident: Ident,
    pub colon_token: Token![:],
    pub ty: Box<Type>,
    pub eq_token: Token![=],
    pub expr: Box<Expr>,
    pub semi_token: Token![;],
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing)Parsing

Keywords and punctuation can be parsed through the [ ParseStream::parse](https://docs.rs/parse/struct.ParseBuffer.html#method.parse)
method. Delimiter tokens are parsed using the

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)

`parenthesized!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)

`bracketed!`[macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)

`braced!````
use syn::{Attribute, Result};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream};
// Parse the ItemStatic struct shown above.
impl Parse for ItemStatic {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        Ok(ItemStatic {
            attrs: input.call(Attribute::parse_outer)?,
            vis: input.parse()?,
            static_token: input.parse()?,
            mutability: input.parse()?,
            ident: input.parse()?,
            colon_token: input.parse()?,
            ty: input.parse()?,
            eq_token: input.parse()?,
            expr: input.parse()?,
            semi_token: input.parse()?,
        })
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#other-operations)Other operations

Every keyword and punctuation token supports the following operations.

# syn::visit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0.118/syn/visit/index.html

**crate feature**only.

`visit`## Expand description

Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.

Each method of the [ Visit](https://docs.rs/trait.Visit.html) trait is a hook that can be overridden to
customize the behavior when visiting the corresponding type of node. By
default, every method recursively visits the substructure of the input
by invoking the right visitor method of each of its fields.

```
pub trait Visit<'ast> {
    /* ... */
    fn visit_expr_binary(&mut self, node: &'ast ExprBinary) {
        visit_expr_binary(self, node);
    }
    /* ... */
}
pub fn visit_expr_binary<'ast, V>(v: &mut V, node: &'ast ExprBinary)
where
    V: Visit<'ast> + ?Sized,
{
    for attr in &node.attrs {
        v.visit_attribute(attr);
    }
    v.visit_expr(&*node.left);
    v.visit_bin_op(&node.op);
    v.visit_expr(&*node.right);
}
/* ... */
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This visitor will print the name of every freestanding function in the syntax tree, including nested functions.

```
// [dependencies]
// quote = "1.0"
// syn = { version = "2.0", features = ["full", "visit"] }
use quote::quote;
use syn::visit::{self, Visit};
use syn::{File, ItemFn};
struct FnVisitor;
impl<'ast> Visit<'ast> for FnVisitor {
    fn visit_item_fn(&mut self, node: &'ast ItemFn) {
        println!("Function with name={}", node.sig.ident);
        // Delegate to the default impl to visit any nested functions.
        visit::visit_item_fn(self, node);
    }
}
fn main() {
    let code = quote! {
        pub fn f() {
            fn g() {}
        }
    };
    let syntax_tree: File = syn::parse2(code).unwrap();
    FnVisitor.visit_file(&syntax_tree);
}
```
The `'ast` lifetime on the input references means that the syntax tree
outlives the complete recursive visit call, so the visitor is allowed to
hold on to references into the syntax tree.

```
use quote::quote;
use syn::visit::{self, Visit};
use syn::{File, ItemFn};
struct FnVisitor<'ast> {
    functions: Vec<&'ast ItemFn>,
}
impl<'ast> Visit<'ast> for FnVisitor<'ast> {
    fn visit_item_fn(&mut self, node: &'ast ItemFn) {
        self.functions.push(node);
        visit::visit_item_fn(self, node);
    }
}
fn main() {
    let code = quote! {
        pub fn f() {
            fn g() {}
        }
    };
    let syntax_tree: File = syn::parse2(code).unwrap();
    let mut visitor = FnVisitor { functions: Vec::new() };
    visitor.visit_file(&syntax_tree);
    for f in visitor.functions {
        println!("Function with name={}", f.sig.ident);
    }
}
```

- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.

# syn::visit_mut - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0.118/syn/visit_mut/index.html

**crate feature**only.

`visit-mut`## Expand description

Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

Each method of the [ VisitMut](https://docs.rs/trait.VisitMut.html) trait is a hook that can be overridden
to customize the behavior when mutating the corresponding type of node.
By default, every method recursively visits the substructure of the
input by invoking the right visitor method of each of its fields.

```
pub trait VisitMut {
    /* ... */
    fn visit_expr_binary_mut(&mut self, node: &mut ExprBinary) {
        visit_expr_binary_mut(self, node);
    }
    /* ... */
}
pub fn visit_expr_binary_mut<V>(v: &mut V, node: &mut ExprBinary)
where
    V: VisitMut + ?Sized,
{
    for attr in &mut node.attrs {
        v.visit_attribute_mut(attr);
    }
    v.visit_expr_mut(&mut *node.left);
    v.visit_bin_op_mut(&mut node.op);
    v.visit_expr_mut(&mut *node.right);
}
/* ... */
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This mut visitor replace occurrences of u256 suffixed integer literals
like `999u256` with a macro invocation `bigint::u256!(999)`.

```
// [dependencies]
// quote = "1.0"
// syn = { version = "2.0", features = ["full", "visit-mut"] }
use quote::quote;
use syn::visit_mut::{self, VisitMut};
use syn::{parse_quote, Expr, File, Lit, LitInt};
struct BigintReplace;
impl VisitMut for BigintReplace {
    fn visit_expr_mut(&mut self, node: &mut Expr) {
        if let Expr::Lit(expr) = &node {
            if let Lit::Int(int) = &expr.lit {
                if int.suffix() == "u256" {
                    let digits = int.base10_digits();
                    let unsuffixed: LitInt = syn::parse_str(digits).unwrap();
                    *node = parse_quote!(bigint::u256!(#unsuffixed));
                    return;
                }
            }
        }
        // Delegate to the default impl to visit nested expressions.
        visit_mut::visit_expr_mut(self, node);
    }
}
fn main() {
    let code = quote! {
        fn main() {
            let _ = 999u256;
        }
    };
    let mut syntax_tree: File = syn::parse2(code).unwrap();
    BigintReplace.visit_file_mut(&mut syntax_tree);
    println!("{}", quote!(#syntax_tree));
}
```
## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Visit](https://docs.rs/trait.VisitMut.html)- Mut
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

# Token in syn - Rust
